title: The rivet that made Levi's jeans
hook: Blue jeans began with a Nevada tailor who could not afford a patent.
peek: In the early 1870s a tailor in Reno started hammering copper rivets into the pocket corners of work trousers. He needed a partner to pay for the patent, so he wrote to his fabric supplier, Levi Strauss.
lede: Levi Strauss did not invent jeans. A tailor named Jacob Davis, working in Reno, Nevada, began reinforcing the stress points of work trousers with copper rivets, the kind used on horse blankets. His customers loved them. He could not afford to patent the idea alone, so he wrote to Strauss, the San Francisco merchant who sold him his cloth.

bullets.text: Davis and Levi Strauss & Co. received a US patent for riveted pocket openings on 20 May 1873. That date is now treated as the birthday of blue jeans, and Davis moved to San Francisco to oversee production.

bullets.opening: A request from a customer's wife
bullets.text: The story goes that a woman asked Davis for trousers that would survive her husband's work. Davis himself described it this way, so it is a better source than most clothing legends, but it is still one man's account.
Rivets on the back pockets scratched saddles, chairs and car seats. In the 1930s the company covered them with fabric, and later it dropped them. The front-pocket rivets stayed.

Denim is usually traced to serge de Nîmes, a cloth from the French city, and jeans to Genoa, whose sailors wore sturdy cotton trousers. Both are standard dictionary explanations, though the early history of the fabrics is murky.
The rivet is a simple fastener that turned an ordinary garment into a durable one. Velcro did something similar about eighty years later, starting from a walk in the woods.
Jeans kept the button fly long after zips arrived, and the 501 still uses one. Buttons have their own riddle: why men's and women's garments fasten on opposite sides.
